1275.title: Friendship prayer (Life 8)
1275.hook: Teresa: mental prayer is friendly conversation, often alone, with him who loves us
1275.howItsDone: Catholics who follow Teresa's teaching set aside regular time, often daily, for mental prayer: quiet, personal conversation with God, frequently in front of the tabernacle or with a Gospel passage open.

segments.voice: Yesterday, The Way of Perfection, and Teresa's three foundations: love, detachment, humility, laid down before any talk of prayer. Your line was three foundations.

"And the Lord spoke to Moses face to face, as a man is wont to speak to his friend." That line from Exodus, in the Douay-Rheims, describes God and a human being talking the way friends do. Teresa of Ávila spent years in a convent before prayer felt anything like that. In her autobiography, the Life, she admits that during the hour of prayer she sometimes paid more attention to waiting for the hour to end than to anything holy. Yet in that same chapter she describes prayer so plainly it fits in one breath. You heard the idea on day twenty; today, the chapter it comes from.
screen: `FACE TO FACE, AS WITH A FRIEND.` → `TERESA WAITS FOR THE HOUR TO END.` → `YET SHE DEFINES PRAYER PLAINLY.`

segments.voice: Mental prayer sounds like something done in the head, a mind exercise. Teresa means something warmer. In chapter eight of the Life she says that mental prayer, as she sees it, is nothing other than a friendly conversation, often spent alone, with the one we know loves us. Every piece matters. Friendly: not a performance, not an exam. Conversation: two sides, so listening as well as talking. Often alone: time apart, the way you'd step out of a crowded room to talk to someone properly. And the hinge: with the one we know loves us. The friendship starts from his side. Jesus says it at the Last Supper, in John's Gospel: "But I have called you friends." Teresa is honest that the friendship can feel lopsided. She knew her own unfaithfulness, and in the same chapter she describes years of picking prayer up and dropping it. Her conclusion isn't that prayer is for saints. It's the opposite. She urges anyone who has started never to give it up, and anyone who hasn't to begin, because a friend who keeps showing up is never wasted time, even on the days the conversation is thin. Catholics distinguish mental prayer from vocal prayer, set words said aloud, like the rosary, but Teresa doesn't set them against each other. Words said with attention to whom you're speaking already lean toward mental prayer. The point is the attention, and the friendship underneath it.
screen: `NOT A MIND EXERCISE.` · `A FRIENDLY CONVERSATION, OFTEN ALONE.` · `WITH THE ONE WE KNOW LOVES US.` · `KEEP SHOWING UP, EVEN ON THIN DAYS.` · then, large: `BUT I HAVE CALLED YOU FRIENDS.`

segments.voice: If you pray, talk to God the way you'd talk to a close friend across a kitchen table, what happened, what worries you, what you're grateful for, then stop and leave room for the other side. If you don't pray, bring to mind a friend who knows you well, and notice how different it is to speak to someone who already loves you. No need to sound holy.
Mental prayer. For Teresa, a friendly conversation, often alone, with the one we know loves us. Today's word.
Your line: friendly conversation. Even on the days it's thin, showing up is never wasted. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1276.title: A prayer that isn't hers
1276.hook: Christ has no body now but yours is widely credited to Teresa but doesn't appear in her writings
1276.howItsDone: Catholics who study the saints read their words in critical editions of their writings, and Carmelite scholars note which popular sayings attributed to Teresa are not found there.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mental prayer: for Teresa, a friendly conversation, often alone, with the one we know loves us. Your line was friendly conversation.

A bookmark in a parish gift shop. A poster in a hospital chapel. A slide at the end of a volunteer training. The words are lovely: Christ has no body now on earth but yours, no hands but yours, no feet but yours. And underneath, in small italic letters, a name: Teresa of Ávila. It's a prayer people print, frame and read aloud at funerals. There's only one problem with the name at the bottom, and someone who loves Teresa might care about it.
screen: `ON BOOKMARKS AND POSTERS.` → `CHRIST HAS NO BODY NOW BUT YOURS.` → `SIGNED: TERESA OF ÁVILA?`

segments.voice: The lines don't appear in Teresa's writings. Readers have looked through her Life, The Way of Perfection, The Interior Castle, her Foundations and her letters, and the prayer isn't there. Where it did come from isn't settled. So the name on the bookmark is a guess that hardened into a label. Does that make the prayer bad? No. Its idea runs straight back to Saint Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "Now you are the body of Christ, and members of member." Catholics can treasure the thought and use it. The only thing wrong is the signature. Now compare a short verse that tradition does connect with her. It was found, the story goes, in her breviary, the book she prayed from, written in Spanish. It begins, let nothing disturb you, let nothing frighten you, and it ends, God alone is enough. Same saint, two paths to us: one with a trail you can follow, one without. Why care? Because a saint's real voice is worth hearing on its own terms. Teresa's own writing can be funny, sharp and demanding in ways a gift-shop quote is not. And Scripture itself praises checking. The book of Acts describes the people of Berea, who heard Paul gladly but went home "daily searching the scriptures, whether these things were so." Paul tells another church: "prove all things; hold fast that which is good." Checking a source isn't cynicism. It's a way of taking the words, and the person, seriously.

1277.title: Teresa's humor
1277.hook: stories of her wit, like praying to be delivered from sour-faced saints
1277.howItsDone: Carmelites and other readers of Teresa often point to her warmth and wit, and her line about finding the Lord among the pots and pans is quoted in homilies on holiness in ordinary work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a prayer that isn't hers: lovely lines with the wrong signature. Your line was check the source.

Here's a story people tell about Teresa. She's traveling in a rough cart to found another convent. The cart tips, and she ends up in a cold, muddy river. Soaked, she complains to God, and hears him say that this is how he treats his friends. And she answers: then no wonder you have so few. True? After yesterday, the honest answer is that it's a story people tell, not something from her books. But stories like it cluster around her for a reason. People remembered a saint who could laugh.
screen: `A CART, A RIVER, A COMPLAINT.` → `NO WONDER YOU HAVE SO FEW.` → `A STORY, NOT HER BOOKS.`

segments.voice: Another saying comes down under her name: a prayer to be delivered from silly devotions and from sour-faced saints. Like the river story, hold it as tradition. But the spirit behind both is all over her real writing. In her Foundations, she's teaching sisters who felt guilty for being stuck with chores instead of long hours in the chapel. Her answer is warm and practical: if obedience has you in the kitchen, remember the Lord walks among the pots and pans. That's Teresa. She takes God with total seriousness, and herself much less so. Her pages have asides that poke fun at her own memory, her own rambling, her own tangled explanations. Why might a saint's humor matter? One way to see it: sourness can be a quiet form of pride. A sour face is often keeping score, of its own sacrifices and everyone else's failures. Humor lets go of the score. Earlier this week Teresa named humility the chief foundation, and laughing at yourself is humility with a lighter touch. Scripture leaves room for this. Paul writes to the Philippians, in the Douay-Rheims: "Rejoice in the Lord always; again, I say, rejoice." And to the Corinthians: "for God loveth a cheerful giver." Not a grim giver, not one who sighs loudly. A cheerful one. None of this means faking it on a hard day. Teresa had plenty of those, and wrote about them. It means refusing to let holiness curdle into a frown.

1278.title: John's counsels
1278.hook: short sayings for daily life from John of the Cross
1278.howItsDone: Readers of John of the Cross often keep one of his Sayings of Light and Love on a card or in a breviary, and Carmelites read them for short meditations.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Teresa's humor: God among the pots and pans, and a saint who took herself lightly. Your line was not sour-faced.

John of the Cross has a reputation. He's the Carmelite friar of the dark night: long poems, dense commentaries, the soul stripped of everything. You first met him on day two hundred fifty-four, the small friar. People who haven't read him sometimes picture someone stern and far away. But he was Teresa's companion in the reform of Carmel, and he guided other people, friars, nuns and lay people, one conversation at a time. For them he wrote something that fits in a pocket: short sayings, a sentence or two each.
screen: `THE FRIAR OF THE DARK NIGHT.` → `TERESA'S COMPANION, A GUIDE.` → `SAYINGS THAT FIT IN A POCKET.`

segments.voice: Counsels are advice, the kind a guide gives someone they know. Some of John's are gathered under the title Sayings of Light and Love, and tradition says he would sometimes hand them to people written on small slips of paper. Take one. In his own Spanish: a la tarde te examinarán en el amor. In the evening, you will be examined on love. The evening of a day, or the evening of a life, isn't judged on how much you got done, how holy you looked, how many prayers you said. The exam has one subject. It fits the Bible John knew so well, the first letter of John, in the Douay-Rheims: "God is charity: and he that abideth in charity, abideth in God, and God in him." A second counsel comes from one of his letters to a Carmelite nun, written at a hard time. His advice, roughly: where there is no love, put love, and you will draw love out. Not wait for love. Not complain about its absence. Put it there, first, yourself. That's John at his most practical, and it's the same man who wrote the dark night. The night, for John, is about love too: being emptied so that love has room. The sayings are the daytime version: small enough to tape to a mirror, and hard enough to keep a reader busy for a lifetime.

segments.voice: Take this saying, in the evening, you will be examined on love, and say it slowly in your head. Then look back over today, or yesterday if it's early, and ask only: where was love, and where was it missing? If you pray, offer God what you find; if you don't, let the question sit without an answer.

1279.title: The desert houses
1279.hook: Carmelites keep times of deep silence and solitude
1279.howItsDone: Carmelite communities keep regular times of deeper silence and solitude, sometimes called desert days, and some Carmelite friars have houses set apart for longer periods of retreat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, John's counsels, short sayings like in the evening, you will be examined on love. Your line was counsels.

Mark's Gospel describes a long day in Capernaum. Jesus heals a fever, and by sunset the whole town seems to be crowded at the door with its sick. Then, in the Douay-Rheims: "And rising very early, going out, he went into a desert place: and there he prayed." His friends come hunting for him, and when they find him, they say it plainly: "All seek for thee." Before the next town, before the next crowd, he goes to a quiet place first. Carmelites took that pattern and gave it buildings.
screen: `A CROWDED DAY IN CAPERNAUM.` → `VERY EARLY, A DESERT PLACE.` → `ALL SEEK FOR THEE.`

segments.voice: A desert, in Carmelite language, doesn't need sand. It's a place set apart for silence and solitude. In the reformed branch of the order, friars founded houses they called deserts, set apart from busy places, where a friar could withdraw for a season and live closer to the hermits of the first Carmel: a cell, long hours of prayer, very little talk. The idea comes straight out of the Rule from a few days ago. The Rule asks for silence, and it quotes the prophet Isaiah, in the Douay-Rheims: "in silence and in hope shall your strength be." Silence there isn't emptiness. It's where strength is gathered. The prophet Hosea gives the desert a tenderness, too. God says of his people: "I will allure her, and will lead her into the wilderness: and I will speak to her heart." The wilderness is where the speaking happens, because nothing else is talking. Some Carmelite communities still keep desert days and times of deeper retreat, and lay people who follow Carmel sometimes make their own. Notice the rhythm, though. Jesus goes to the desert place, and then he goes back out, to the next towns. The desert isn't an escape from people. It's a return to the source, so there's something to give them. A desert house may be far away. But an hour without noise, a walk without headphones, a room with the door shut, can do a small version of the same work.

1280.title: The elevator
1280.hook: Thérèse, too small to climb the stairs of perfection, looks for a lift: Jesus's arms
1280.howItsDone: Catholics who follow Thérèse's little way read Story of a Soul and try to bring small daily acts to God with childlike trust, rather than measuring their own spiritual progress.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the desert houses: Carmel's places of deep silence, and Jesus rising early for a desert place. Your line was the desert.

A steep, rough staircase, and at the bottom someone very small, looking up at it. That's the picture a young French Carmelite, Thérèse of Lisieux, used for herself when she looked at the saints. They seemed to her like mountains, and she like a grain of sand. She could have given up there, or gritted her teeth and climbed harder. Thérèse did neither. She went looking for a machine. You met it briefly on day ninety-three; today, how she built it.
screen: `A STEEP STAIRCASE, A SMALL CHILD.` → `SAINTS LIKE MOUNTAINS, SHE LIKE SAND.` → `SHE LOOKS FOR A MACHINE.`

segments.voice: In the pages later published as Story of a Soul, Thérèse writes that she lives in an age of inventions. In wealthy homes, people no longer bother with the stairs: a lift carries them up. She wants one too, a lift to Jesus, because she is too little to climb the rough stairway of perfection. So she goes looking in Scripture, and she finds two lines. The first is from Proverbs, in the Douay-Rheims: "Whosoever is a little one, let him come to me." The second is from the end of Isaiah, God speaking as a mother: "As one whom the mother caresseth, so will I comfort you." Isaiah adds that the little ones will be carried and dandled on the knees. Then comes her conclusion, the turn the whole image is built for. The elevator, she says, is your arms, Jesus. And for that, she doesn't need to grow up. She needs to stay little, and become more so. That's the heart of what she called her little way. Notice what it isn't. It isn't laziness: Thérèse worked hard and kept a demanding Rule. It isn't pretending to be helpless. It's a change in who does the lifting. Effort stays, but the anxious grading of your own spiritual height goes. Jesus says something close in Matthew: "unless you be converted, and become as little children, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven." The little way might sound like this: I can't climb this by myself. I'll keep taking the small steps, and let myself be carried.

1281.title: My vocation is love
1281.hook: Thérèse finds her place in the Church's heart
1281.carry: love in the heart of the church
1281.howItsDone: Catholics who love Thérèse read this passage of Story of a Soul and try to offer small, hidden acts of love in ordinary life, her way of being love in the heart of the Church.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the elevator: Thérèse, too small for the stairs, carried up in the arms of Jesus. Your line was carried up.

What do you want to be? Thérèse's answer was: everything. Inside the walls of a small Carmel in Normandy, she writes that she feels drawn to every calling at once. A warrior for the Church. A priest. An apostle traveling the world. A teacher. A martyr. Each desire pulls in a different direction, and she can't live any of them from a convent cell. The wanting itself, she says, becomes a kind of suffering. So she does what she did with the staircase. She opens her Bible.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU WANT TO BE?` → `EVERYTHING, AT ONCE.` → `SHE OPENS HER BIBLE.`

segments.voice: She turns to Saint Paul's first letter to the Corinthians, chapters twelve and thirteen. Paul describes the Church as one body with many members. Some are apostles, some prophets, some teachers, and he asks whether all are apostles. Not everyone can be everything. Thérèse reads the list, and doesn't find herself in it. She keeps reading. Paul goes on to a more excellent way, and the chapter about charity, ending, "the greatest of these is charity." And something opens. If the Church is a body, she reasons, it must have a heart, and that heart burns with love. Love is what moves every other member. Without it, apostles would stop preaching and martyrs would refuse to shed their blood. Love holds every vocation inside it. Then she writes the line in her own French: ma vocation, c'est l'amour. My vocation is love. In the heart of the Church, her mother, she will be love. And so she'll be everything she dreamed of, without leaving the cell. Then, because this is Thérèse, she brings it down to size. She can't do great deeds, so she'll do small ones: a smile, a kind word, a sacrifice no one sees, given like flowers scattered before a king. That's the link to yesterday. The little way isn't small in its aim. It aims at the heart of everything, one small act at a time.
screen: `THE CHURCH IS A BODY.` · `SHE ISN'T IN PAUL'S LIST.` · `A BODY MUST HAVE A HEART.` · `SMALL ACTS, SCATTERED LIKE FLOWERS.` · then, large: `MY VOCATION IS LOVE.`

segments.voice: Think of the next ordinary task waiting for you, dishes, an email, a drive, a diaper, and decide to do that one thing with love, as a quiet gift to someone, without announcing it. If you pray, offer it ahead of time, the way Thérèse offered her small acts; if you don't, just picture yourself doing it gently, fully, and well.
